extracted.intended_audience: after-dinner speakers, club orators, public speakers and humorists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical techniques for composing and delivering after-dinner and impromptu-style speeches that seem spontaneous, amuse an audience, and leave a memorable takeaway.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, tell the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a compact maxim the speaker uses as a dependable rescue in emergencies and times of tribulation; recommended as a single serious takeaway to include in a speech so listeners have something useful to carry home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare an 'impromptu' in advance (simulate spontaneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: To do an impromptu speech as it should be done you have to write it ahead, get it by heart, and indicate the places for pauses and hesitations and the places for applause so the delivery appears spontaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method: begin about a week ahead, write out the speech, memorize it, mark pauses/hesitations and applause cues in the text so that the audience is deceived into believing the speech is offhand. The narrator claims this art makes the speech fully convincing as impromptu and explains why his versions appeared in print differently from others'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the introducer or provocation as your 'text'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the man who introduces you derides or attacks you, he furnishes you with a text (a provocation) to speak against; conversely, if the introducer merely tells the truth about you, you may have no text to work from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for speakers: welcome (or exploit) hostile or pointed introductions because they supply material and a clear rhetorical angle; when no such provocation exists, prepare your own 'text' or theme in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speaking on compliments alone
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot talk on compliments; that is not a text. No modest person can talk on compliments—the speaker is filled with emotion and his tongue is tied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on being given only compliments as the framework for a talk; a string of compliments leaves the speaker without a usable theme or driving idea, so either obtain a substantive text or delay until you have material to speak from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least one serious, carry-home maxim in an after-dinner speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sitting down, say one serious word which the audience can carry home and relate to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in a levity-filled after-dinner address, conclude (or include) a concise serious maxim (example given: 'When in doubt, tell the truth') so the audience leaves with something of lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't preface a read lecture with a memorized poetic passage if interruptions are likely
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to preface a manuscript lecture with a memorized, poetical introductory passage is risky because interruptions (household calls, announcements, etc.) can repeatedly break the delivery and ruin the lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of Dr. Hayes: repeated interruptions during an ornate memorized preface destroyed the lecture. Lesson—either avoid elaborate memorized prefaces when interruptions are possible, or prepare to adapt to interruptions and not depend on uninterrupted recitation.
